claim: Movement-correlated brain activity has been found across species and brain regions.
source: Movement-correlated brain activity has been found across species and brain regions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract summarizing existing knowledge in the field.

claim: Fast whole brain lightfield imaging was used in adult Drosophila to investigate the relationship between walk and brain-wide neuronal activity.
source: Here, we used fast whole brain lightfield imaging in adult Drosophila to investigate the relationship between walk and brain-wide neuronal activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: A global change in activity was observed that tightly correlated with spontaneous bouts of walk.
source: We observed a global change in activity that tightly correlated with spontaneous bouts of walk.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental observations.

claim: Imaging specific sets of excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory neurons highlighted their joint contribution to walk-related activity.
source: While imaging specific sets of excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory neurons highlighted their joint contribution, spatial heterogeneity in walk- and turning-induced activity allowed parsing unique responses from subregions and sometimes individual candidate neurons.
evidence: This describes findings from imaging experiments with specific neuron types.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity in walk- and turning-induced activity allowed parsing unique responses from subregions and sometimes individual candidate neurons.
source: While imaging specific sets of excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory neurons highlighted their joint contribution, spatial heterogeneity in walk- and turning-induced activity allowed parsing unique responses from subregions and sometimes individual candidate neurons.
evidence: This describes the ability to distinguish responses in different brain regions.

claim: Previously uncharacterized serotonergic neurons were inhibited during walk.
source: For example, previously uncharacterized serotonergic neurons were inhibited during walk.
evidence: This is a specific finding about serotonergic neuron activity during walking.

claim: Activity onset in some areas preceded walk onset exclusively in spontaneously walking animals.
source: While activity onset in some areas preceded walk onset exclusively in spontaneously walking animals, spontaneous and forced walk elicited similar activity in most brain regions.
evidence: This describes temporal relationships between neural activity and behavior onset.

claim: Spontaneous and forced walk elicited similar activity in most brain regions.
source: While activity onset in some areas preceded walk onset exclusively in spontaneously walking animals, spontaneous and forced walk elicited similar activity in most brain regions.
evidence: This compares neural activity patterns between spontaneous and forced walking conditions.

claim: Walk and walk-related sensory or proprioceptive information contribute majorly to global activity of all major neuronal classes.
source: These data suggest a major contribution of walk and walk-related sensory or proprioceptive information to global activity of all major neuronal classes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Recent work in mice showed that multiple dimensions of spontaneous behavior, including facial or body movements, are represented brain-wide.
source: Using a combination of imaging and neuropixel recordings in awake, behaving mice, recent work showed that multiple dimensions of (spontaneous) behavior, including facial or body movements, are represented brain-wide, allowing the integration of external or internal stimuli with the current behavioral state (Macé et al., 2018; Musall et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: This cites previous studies in mice.

claim: Brain-wide imaging at single cell resolution of calcium activity in C. elegans and larval zebrafish indicated that multiple aspects of behavior and motor activity are represented across the brain including areas thought to be dedicated to primary sensory information processing.
source: Brain-wide imaging at single cell resolution of calcium activity in C. elegans and larval zebrafish indicated that as in mammals, multiple aspects of behavior and motor activity are represented across the brain including areas thought to be dedicated to primary sensory information processing (Kato et al., 2015; Marques et al., 2020; Vladimirov et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites previous studies in C. elegans and zebrafish.

claim: Brain-wide representations of motor states are observed independently of visual or olfactory inputs.
source: Importantly, such brain-wide representations of motor states are observed independently of visual or olfactory inputs.
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous studies.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, active flight modulates visual motion processing.
source: For example, in Drosophila melanogaster, active flight modulates visual motion processing (Maimon et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites a previous study on flight and visual processing in flies.

claim: Visual horizontal system cells encode quantitative information about the fly's walking behavior independently of visual input.
source: Similarly, visual horizontal system cells encode quantitative information about the fly's walking behavior independently of visual input (Fujiwara et al., 2017).
evidence: This cites a previous study on visual system cells and walking.

claim: Several types of dopaminergic neurons innervating the fly's mushroom body show activity highly correlated with bouts of walking.
source: Beyond primary sensory brain areas, several types of dopaminergic neurons innervating the fly's higher brain center, the mushroom body (MB), show activity highly correlated with bouts of walking (Siju et al., 2020; Zolin et al., 2021).
evidence: This cites previous studies on dopaminergic neurons and walking.

claim: Whole brain imaging revealed that behavior-related activity occurred in most brain regions and was independent of visual or olfactory input.
source: Importantly, whole brain imaging revealed that behavior-related activity occurred in most brain regions and was independent of visual or olfactory input (Aimon et al., 2019; Mann et al., 2021; Schaffer et al., 2021).
evidence: This cites previous whole brain imaging studies.

claim: The identity of the specific neuron types and neurotransmitters involved in behavior-related activity as well as where and how behavior-related information is relayed to the brain remain largely unanswered questions.
source: However, the identity of the specific neuron types and neurotransmitters involved as well as where and how behavior-related information is relayed to the brain remain largely unanswered questions.
evidence: This identifies gaps in current knowledge.

claim: The fly provides opportunities to study adult, global brain states associated with behavior at high temporal and spatial resolution due to its small brain size.
source: Complementary to other animal models, the fly provides opportunities to study adult, global brain states associated with behavior at high temporal and spatial resolution due to its small brain size (Aimon and Grunwald Kadow, 2019).
evidence: This explains the advantages of using Drosophila as a model system.

claim: Recent electron microscopy connectomics highlighted that neural networks spread across the entire brain with many pathways unrevealed by traditional single neuron manipulation experiments.
source: In addition, recent electron microscopy (EM) connectomics highlighted that neural networks spread across the entire brain with many pathways unrevealed by traditional single neuron manipulation experiments (Scheffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This cites recent connectomics work.

claim: Adult Drosophila behavior has been studied in detail for many years.
source: Adult Drosophila behavior has been studied in detail for many years (Berman et al., 2016; Calhoun et al., 2019; DeAngelis et al., 2019; Geurten et al., 2014; Katsov et al., 2017; Mendes et al., 2014; Mueller et al., 2019; Tao et al., 2019; Tsai and Chou, 2019), but the resulting or underlying brain-wide activity for even just roughly defined behavioral states such as resting or walking remains mostly unknown.
evidence: This cites previous behavioral studies and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Movement in adult Drosophila is thought to be controlled by descending neurons connecting the brain to the ventral nerve cord (VNC), which contains local pattern generators responsible for movement.
source: Movement in adult Drosophila is thought to be controlled by descending neurons connecting the brain to the ventral nerve cord (VNC), which contains local pattern generators responsible for movement (Bidaye et al., 2020; Bidaye et al., 2014; Emanuel et al., 2020; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Zacarias et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the prevailing model of motor control in flies based on cited studies.

claim: The top-down view of motor control is challenged by other studies suggesting that behavioral control is decentralized with feedback loops involving the brain.
source: This top-down view is challenged by other studies suggesting that behavioral control is decentralized with feedback loops involving the brain (Schilling and Cruse, 2020; Sims et al., 2019), or even that many behaviors could be locally controlled by neurons in the VNC without involving the brain (e.g., decapitated grooming Hirsh, 1997).
evidence: This cites alternative models of motor control.

claim: The fly's head was fixed to a holder with the posterior head capsule opened for optical access while leaving the legs free to move.
source: To image whole brain activity during spontaneous behavior, we fixed the fly's head to a holder, opened the posterior head capsule for optical access while leaving the legs free to move (Woller et al., 2021; Figure 1A), and used a ball as a walkable surface (Seelig et al., 2010; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation method.

claim: GCaMP was expressed pan-neuronally and calcium transients in the neuropil were imaged as a proxy of neuronal activity in the whole brain using fast light field microscopy.
source: We expressed GCaMP pan-neuronally and imaged calcium transients in the neuropil as a proxy of neuronal activity in the whole brain using fast light field microscopy (LFM) as described previously (Aimon et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the imaging method and calcium indicator used.

claim: Light field microscopy recordings of neuropil were at a typical scale of 5 µm.
source: This resulted in recordings of neuropil at a typical scale of 5 µm (Aimon et al., 2019).
evidence: This specifies the spatial resolution of the imaging.

claim: The R2 represents the fraction of variance explained by the behavior and will decrease with noisier signals.
source: The R2, representing the fraction of variance explained by the behavior, will decrease with noisier signals (such as those from flies with low GCaMP expression levels).
evidence: This explains the properties of the R2 metric.

claim: The coefficient represents the intensity and sign of the relationship between activity and behavior and will not have the same dependence to noise as R2.
source: By contrast, the coefficient, representing the intensity and sign of the relationship between activity and behavior, will not have the same dependance to noise (its value will be less precise with higher noise).
evidence: This explains the properties of the coefficient metric.

claim: A variety of GCaMP sensors (UAS-GCaMP6s/6m/6f/7s/7f) and frame rates were used to capture both high speed and low signal-to-noise transients.
source: We used a variety of GCaMP sensors (UAS-GCaMP6s/6m/6f/7s/7f) and frame rates to capture both high speed and low signal-to-noise transients.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to optimize imaging.

claim: No significant difference was found in R2 at different frame rates (5–98 Hz) for flies expressing GCaMP pan-neuronally (N = 12 flies).
source: With our data (N = 12 flies), we found no significant difference between the R2 at different frame rates (5–98 Hz) for flies expressing GCaMP pan-neuronally (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and thus pooled these data for the analysis below regarding global brain state.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from comparing different recording conditions.

claim: A strong increase in neuronal activity across the brain was observed during bouts of walking compared to during resting or grooming.
source: We observed a strong increase in neuronal activity across the brain during bouts of walking compared to during resting or grooming (Video 1, Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: The first principal component (PC1) of the whole brain activity data was strongly correlated to walk in experiments where the fly was both walking and resting.
source: Accordingly, in experiments where the fly was both walking and resting, the first principal component (PC1) of the whole brain activity data was strongly correlated to walk (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from principal component analysis of the data.

claim: The global activity of individual brain regions correlated with walk.
source: By aligning whole brain imaging data to the JFR2018 fly brain template using landmark registration, and by averaging activity in each large anatomically defined region (see Methods), we also found that the global activity of individual brain regions correlated with walk (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from region-based analysis of the imaging data.

claim: Neuronal activation followed movement bouts at high temporal precision (limited by the temporal resolution of the calcium reporter) inconsistent with activity generated by slower general arousal such as wake and sleep.
source: Neuronal activation followed movement bouts at high temporal precision (limited by the temporal resolution of the calcium reporter) inconsistent with activity generated by slower general arousal such as wake and sleep (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is an observation about the temporal dynamics of neural activity relative to behavior.

claim: Calcium responses were slower than some of the fast changes in walking, even after convolution of walking with the GCaMP impulse response.
source: However, calcium responses were still a little slower than some of the fast changes in walking, even after convolution of walking with the GCaMP impulse response, which suggests that faster probes could capture finer dynamics in further studies (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation about the temporal limitations of the calcium indicator.

claim: Using walking behavior, approximately 20% of all variances observed in the experiments could be explained (R2 median = 0.194).
source: Nevertheless, using walking behavior we were able to explain ~20% of all variances observed in the experiments (R2 median = 0.194, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the regression analysis.

claim: The global activity correlated primarily with walk and not with the start or end of walk.
source: Moreover, the global activity correlated primarily with walk and not with the start or end of walk (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different behavioral regressors.

claim: Unlike grooming, which resulted in local activation of ventral brain areas, all brain regions were significantly positively correlated with walking.
source: Strikingly, unlike grooming, which resulted in local activation of ventral brain areas consistent with (Hampel et al., 2015 and Robie et al., 2017), all brain regions were significantly positively correlated with walking (Figure 1E, G).
evidence: This compares the spatial patterns of neural activity during different behaviors.

claim: An increase in activity was observed during bouts of flailing, but the brain was not as consistently globally activated as during walking.
source: While we still observed an increase in activity during bouts of flailing, the brain was not as consistently globally activated as during walking in our hands (Figure 1E, G, see also Schaffer et al., 2021).
evidence: This compares neural activity during flailing versus walking.

claim: Two different pan-neuronal lines (nsyb-Gal4 and GMR57C10-Gal4) were used to ensure results were not biased by heterogeneous expression in the pan-neuronal transgenic driver line.
source: To ensure our results were not biased by heterogeneous expression in the pan-neuronal transgenic driver line, we used two different pan-neuronal lines (nsyb-Gal4 and GMR57C10-Gal4).
evidence: This describes a control experiment to validate findings.

claim: The linear model showed that there was no significant effect of the Gal4-driver on the correlation between brain activity and walking.
source: The linear model (Table 1) showed that there was no significant effect of the Gal4-driver.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear model analysis.

claim: A small but significant effect of the GCaMP version used was found, likely reflecting the higher signal to noise ratio for GCaMP6s and GCaMP7s.
source: We found a small but significant effect of the GCaMP version used, likely reflecting the higher signal to noise ratio for GCaMP6s and GCaMP7s, and thus kept using the model to take this effect into account for the rest of the study.
evidence: This is a statistical finding and interpretation about the effect of different GCaMP versions.

claim: All brain areas were significantly activated during walk.
source: While all brain areas were significantly activated during walk (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), only the ventral regions (AMMC, GNG, IPS, IVLP, and SAD; see Table 2 and Ito et al., 2014 for meaning of acronyms) showed significant correlation with grooming (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,H).
evidence: This is a finding from the region-based analysis of walk-related activity.

claim: Only the ventral regions (AMMC, GNG, IPS, IVLP, and SAD) showed significant correlation with grooming.
source: While all brain areas were significantly activated during walk (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), only the ventral regions (AMMC, GNG, IPS, IVLP, and SAD; see Table 2 and Ito et al., 2014 for meaning of acronyms) showed significant correlation with grooming (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,H).
evidence: This is a finding from the region-based analysis of grooming-related activity.

claim: Flailing represents an intermediate state with many brain regions activated but less consistently as compared to walk.
source: Flailing represents an intermediate state with many brain regions activated but less consistently as compared to walk (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,G ).
evidence: This characterizes the neural activity pattern during flailing behavior.

claim: With limited visual input (eyes covered with black nail polish), a similar global activity pattern was still observed indicating that visual input is at best a minor contributor to the observed wide brain activity.
source: With this strongly limited visual input, we still observed a similar, global activity pattern indicating that visual input is at best a minor contributor to our observed wide brain activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from a control experiment manipulating visual input.

claim: The global increase in activity during walk is not due to a mismatch between an actual and a predicted visual stimulus.
source: This result also suggests that the global increase in activity during walk is not due to a mismatch between an actual and a predicted visual stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the visual occlusion experiment results.

claim: The comparison of air-supported and styrofoam ball datasets revealed a significant difference in R2 for global brain activity.
source: The comparison of the two datasets revealed a significant difference in R2 for global brain activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), possibly reflecting differences in surface material, or erratic movements of the air-supported ball unrelated to the fly's movements confounding the walk regressor.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different experimental substrates.

claim: The distribution of R2 across brain regions was similar between the two substrate types (cosine similarity = 0.98).
source: While the R2 was globally different, distribution across brain regions was similar between the two substrate types (cosine similarity = 0.98, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of spatial patterns between conditions.

claim: An increase in global brain activity was detected for excitatory and inhibitory types of neurons during walk.
source: Using the same approach and analysis as described above, we detected an increase in global brain activity for excitatory and inhibitory types of neurons (Figure 2A,B), closely following individual walk bouts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from imaging specific neuron types.

claim: All regions significantly responded to walk for all genotypes (Cha-Gal4, Vglut-Gal4, and GAD-Gal4).
source: All regions significantly responded to walk for all genotypes (Figure 2C, D , Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with high similarity in the distribution across regions (cosine similarity: Cha vs. Vglut: 0.98, Cha vs. Gad: 0.99, Vglut vs. Gad: 0.98) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different neurotransmitter-specific neuron types.

claim: There was high similarity in the distribution of walk-related activity across regions for cholinergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurons (cosine similarity: Cha vs. Vglut: 0.98, Cha vs. Gad: 0.99, Vglut vs. Gad: 0.98).
source: All regions significantly responded to walk for all genotypes (Figure 2C, D , Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with high similarity in the distribution across regions (cosine similarity: Cha vs. Vglut: 0.98, Cha vs. Gad: 0.99, Vglut vs. Gad: 0.98) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of spatial patterns across neuron types.

claim: Both inhibitory neurons and excitatory neurons are activated in most brain regions during walk.
source: Together these data show that both inhibitory neurons and excitatory neurons are activated in most brain regions during walk.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the neuron-type specific imaging experiments.

claim: An increase in activity was observed for all neuromodulatory neuron types (dopaminergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic) during walk.
source: While we observed an increase in activity for all neuromodulatory neuron types, serotonergic neurons (Trh-GAL4;UAS-GCaMP6) were significantly less globally activated than dopaminergic (TH, DDC or GMR58E02-GAL4; UAS-GCaMP) and octopaminergic (Tdc-GAL4; UAS-GCaMP6) neurons during spontaneous bouts of walk (Figure 3A,D, Videos 2–4).
evidence: This is a finding from imaging neuromodulatory neuron types.

claim: Serotonergic neurons were significantly less globally activated than dopaminergic and octopaminergic neurons during spontaneous bouts of walk.
source: While we observed an increase in activity for all neuromodulatory neuron types, serotonergic neurons (Trh-GAL4;UAS-GCaMP6) were significantly less globally activated than dopaminergic (TH, DDC or GMR58E02-GAL4; UAS-GCaMP) and octopaminergic (Tdc-GAL4; UAS-GCaMP6) neurons during spontaneous bouts of walk (Figure 3A,D, Videos 2–4).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between different neuromodulatory neuron types.

claim: Maps for individual aminergic lines were distinctly patterned (cosine similarity: TH-DDC vs. Trh: 0.69, Tdc vs. Trh: 0.69, Tdc vs. TH-DDC: 0.93).
source: When we mapped activity to brain regions (Figure 3B), we found that contrary to the pan-neuronal and broad neurotransmitter line results, maps for individual aminergic lines were distinctly patterned (cosine similarity: TH-DDC vs. Trh: 0.69, Tdc vs. Trh: 0.69, Tdc vs. TH-DDC: 0.93, Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of spatial patterns across aminergic neuron types.

claim: Most regions were significantly correlated with walk for all three aminergic types (dopaminergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic).
source: Nevertheless, most regions were significantly correlated with walk for all three aminergic types (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from region-based analysis of aminergic neuron activity.

claim: The strongest correlation for serotoninergic neurons was negative and mapped to the anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum (AVLP) region.
source: Interestingly, the strongest correlation for serotoninergic neurons was negative and mapped to the anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum (AVLP) region (Figure 3B (blue area), Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is a specific finding about serotonergic neuron activity in a particular brain region.

claim: Functional components derived from recorded neuronal activity match anatomical structures without further subdivisions or blurring of anatomical boundaries.
source: Interestingly, almost all functional components derived from recorded neuronal activity matches anatomical structures without further subdivisions or blurring of anatomical boundaries.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between functional and anatomical maps.

claim: The functional data separated the AVLP (anterior ventro-lateral protocerebrum) into smaller subregions suggesting that subregions of the AVLP had different activity signatures.
source: In one exception, our functional data separated a larger region in the lateral neuropil, the AVLP (anterior ventro-lateral protocerebrum), into smaller subregions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, orange box) suggesting that subregions of the AVLP had different activity signatures.
evidence: This is a finding about functional subdivisions within an anatomical region.

claim: Some components identified more than one brain region indicating a strong functional connection between these regions.
source: Of note, some components also identified more than one brain region (i.e., PENP-SLP) indicating a strong functional connection between these regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of components spanning multiple anatomical regions.

claim: The PENP-SLP, PENP-CL, and WPNb-like components connected ventral neuropils to higher areas or vice versa.
source: For example, among the components correlated with spontaneous walk, the PENP-SLP (periesophageal neuropils and superior lateral protocerebrum) and PENP-CL (periesophageal neuropils and clamp) and WPNb-like (bilateral wedge projection neuron-like Coates et al., 2020) components connected ventral neuropils (e.g., GNG) to higher areas or vice versa.
evidence: This describes the anatomical connectivity of specific functional components.

claim: Walk-correlated neuronal activity was found for dopaminergic components in and around the MB (i.e., γ3 compartment as previously observed).
source: For dopaminergic neurons, walk-correlated neuronal activity was found, for instance, for components in and around the MB (i.e., γ3 compartment as previously observed; Cohn et al., 2015; Siju et al., 2020; Zolin et al., 2021), in the central complex (CX; protocerebral bridge [B-DA] and ellipsoid body [EB-DA-like; Kong et al., 2010]), but also in ventral neuropil such as the wedge (WED-DA-like; Liu et al., 2017) and neuropil connecting central regions to the optic lobes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes walk-correlated activity in dopaminergic neurons and cites previous studies.

claim: For octopamine, one particular component connecting the optic lobe and the periesophageal neuropil (OL-PENP) was strongly correlated with walk.
source: For octopamine, one particular component connecting the optic lobe and the periesophageal neuropil (OL-PENP) was strongly correlated with walk, while for serotoninergic neurons the highest R2 was detected for the AVLP and components within (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes walk-correlated activity in octopaminergic neurons.

claim: For serotonergic neurons, the highest R2 was detected for the AVLP and components within.
source: For octopamine, one particular component connecting the optic lobe and the periesophageal neuropil (OL-PENP) was strongly correlated with walk, while for serotoninergic neurons the highest R2 was detected for the AVLP and components within (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes walk-correlated activity in serotonergic neurons.

claim: Most components with significant R2 were positively correlated with walk.
source: Most components with significant R2 were positively correlated with walk (Figure 4B, C), with few exceptions: a specific component within the AVLP mostly detected in the experiment using Trh-Gal4, which we named the AVLPshell due to its shape, was negatively correlated (i.e., inhibited) with walk (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding about the sign of correlation between components and walk.

claim: A specific component within the AVLP (AVLPshell) detected in experiments using Trh-Gal4 was negatively correlated (i.e., inhibited) with walk.
source: Most components with significant R2 were positively correlated with walk (Figure 4B, C), with few exceptions: a specific component within the AVLP mostly detected in the experiment using Trh-Gal4, which we named the AVLPshell due to its shape, was negatively correlated (i.e., inhibited) with walk (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a specific finding about inhibition of serotonergic neurons during walk.

claim: Components that were differentially activated during turning were reproducibly found across different flies based on similar position and morphology.
source: The components that were differentially activated during turning were reproducibly found across different flies based on similar position and morphology (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of turning-related components.

claim: The IPS-Y and LAL-PS components were differentially activated during turning.
source: These included the IPS-Y (inverse Y shape in the posterior slope) and LAL-PS (lateral accessory lobe and posterior slope) as previously mentioned in Aimon et al., 2019.
evidence: This identifies specific components related to turning and cites a previous study.

claim: For dopaminergic neurons, the components most correlated with turning had a shape closely matching the dopaminergic neuron type known to project to the LAL and WED areas: neurons of the PPM2 cluster (PPM2-LW).
source: For dopaminergic neurons, the components most correlated with turning had a shape closely matching the dopaminergic neuron type known to project to the LAL and WED areas: neurons of the PPM2 cluster, that is, PPM2-LW (PPM2-LAL-WED: PPM2-lateral accessory lobe-wedge; Mao and Davis, 2009; Figure 5A, right panels; Video 5).
evidence: This matches a functional component to a known neuron type based on anatomy and cites a previous study.

claim: Regions around the esophagus, such as the posterior slope (IPS-Y, SPS) and the dopaminergic M-Omega component, as well as the WED-DA-like component showed activity that began to increase significantly before walk onset.
source: In particular, we found that regions around the esophagus, such as the posterior slope (IPS-Y, SPS) and the dopaminergic M-Omega component (corresponding to two posterior neuropil regions), as well as the WED-DA-like component showed activity that began to increase significantly before walk onset.
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of neural activity relative to walk onset.

claim: Several compartments of the MB and regions in the superior neuropil regions (e.g., SMP and SLP) showed trials with some increase preceding walk.
source: In addition, several compartments of the MB and regions in the superior neuropil regions (e.g., SMP and SLP) showed trials with some increase preceding walk (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of neural activity in specific brain regions.

claim: The OL-PLP-WED component was activated significantly before walk.
source: The OL-PLP-WED component was also activated significantly before walk.
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of neural activity in a specific component.

claim: Most components that mapped to the CX (comprising the protocerebral bridge, fan-shaped body, ellipsoid body, and noduli) were activated at walk onset but not before.
source: Most components that mapped to the CX (comprising the protocerebral bridge (PB), fan-shaped body (FB), ellipsoid body (EB), and noduli (NO)) were activated at walk onset but not before (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of neural activity in central complex regions.

claim: The components PB–EB and EB–DA became activated once the fly started to walk.
source: In particular, the components PB–EB (connecting the PB and the EB) and EB–DA (comprising neurons in the EB and the lateral accessory lobe) became activated once the fly started to walk (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with an increase at walk onset of dopaminergic activity in the EB and LAL (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of neural activity in specific central complex components.

claim: While anterior and medial components of AVLP increased in activity at walk onset, the AVLPshell component displayed a very clear decrease in neuronal activity as soon as the fly started to walk.
source: While anterior and medial components of AVLP increased in activity at walk onset, the AVLP component that resembled the shape of a shell (AVLPshell) displayed a very clear decrease in neuronal activity as soon as the fly started to walk (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about the timing and direction of neural activity changes in AVLP subregions.

claim: Activity could originate from superior decision-making areas and then spread across the brain (top-down) or be initiated by motor activity and proprioception (bottom-up) and then distribute to higher brain areas.
source: We hypothesized that in the extreme case, activity could originate from two opposite sites. First, the activity could arise initially in superior decision-making areas and then spreads across the brain (top-down) or, second, activity is initiated by motor activity and proprioception (bottom-up) and then distributes to higher brain areas.
evidence: This presents two alternative hypotheses about the origin of walk-related brain activity.

claim: In the bottom-up scenario, activity would originate in the VNC and move to basal regions of the brain, i.e., the GNG, via ascending neurons (ANs).
source: In the latter case, activity would originate in the VNC and move to basal regions of the brain, i.e., the GNG, via ascending neurons (ANs) (Chen et al., 2023; Tsubouchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This elaborates on the bottom-up hypothesis and cites relevant studies.

claim: Most activity was more consistent with a 'bottom-up' scenario based on component analysis of data recorded at 30 Hz.
source: While our component analysis of data recorded at 30 Hz identified several putative 'top-down' components active before walk onset, most activity was more consistent with a 'bottom-up' scenario (Figures 1 and 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing analysis results.

claim: In some trials, the activity detected during walk appeared to progress from areas at the base of the brain (GNG) to more dorsal areas.
source: In some trials, we observed that the activity detected during walk appeared to progress from areas at the base of the brain, that is from GNG to more dorsal areas (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, see Video 6 for an example trial).
evidence: This is an observation about the spatial progression of neural activity.

claim: Compared to cellular-GCaMP, sytGCaMP activity was very strong in the GNG, AMMC, and AVLP, regions receiving inputs from the VNC.
source: Compared to cellular-GCaMP, sytGCaMP activity was very strong in the GNG, AMMC, and AVLP, regions receiving inputs from the VNC (Figure 7A; Tsubouchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing synaptic and cellular GCaMP and cites a study on VNC inputs.

claim: Forced walk induced a change in brain state, with brain-wide activity increases across regions, similar to spontaneous walk.
source: Similarly to spontaneous walk (Figure 7B, D), forced walk induced a change in brain state, with brain-wide activity increases across regions (Figure 7C, D, Video 7, cosine similarity: 0.993 for R2 and 0.985 for the coefficients), and across components (Figure 7E, cosine similarity: 0.87 for R2 and 0.85 for the coefficients).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing spontaneous and forced walk conditions.

claim: Flies with a surgically severed connection between the brain and VNC walked on the treadmill while showing hardly any activity in the brain.
source: In addition, flies with a surgically severed connection between the brain and VNC walked on the treadmill while showing hardly any activity in the brain (Figure 7D, Video 8), consistent with the hypothesis that the brain is not necessary for forced walk and walking signals driving whole brain state change originate in the VNC.
evidence: This is a finding from a lesion experiment supporting the bottom-up hypothesis.

claim: The brain is not necessary for forced walk and walking signals driving whole brain state change originate in the VNC.
source: In addition, flies with a surgically severed connection between the brain and VNC walked on the treadmill while showing hardly any activity in the brain (Figure 7D, Video 8), consistent with the hypothesis that the brain is not necessary for forced walk and walking signals driving whole brain state change originate in the VNC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lesion experiment results.

claim: The observations about similarity between spontaneous and forced walk were true not only for pan-neuronal data but also for dopaminergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic neuronal subsets.
source: Importantly, these observations were not only true for pan-neuronal data but also for dopaminergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic neuronal subsets (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This extends the spontaneous vs. forced walk comparison to specific neuron types.

claim: Confidence intervals were overlapping for all brain regions when comparing forced and spontaneous walk in dopaminergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic neurons.
source: While we did observe some variation between forced and spontaneous walk in the R2 for regression of activity traces with walk, confidence intervals were overlapping for all brain regions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E) and cosine similarity was high (TH-DDC: 0.985 for R2, 0.978 for coefficients, Tdc: 0.96 for R2, 0.93 for coefficients, Trh: 0.84 for R2, 0.62 for coefficients) further suggesting that walking, whether spontaneous or forced, elicits a similar global state change of the brain.
evidence: This is a statistical finding supporting similarity between spontaneous and forced walk.

claim: Cosine similarity was high between spontaneous and forced walk for dopaminergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic neurons (TH-DDC: 0.985 for R2, 0.978 for coefficients, Tdc: 0.96 for R2, 0.93 for coefficients, Trh: 0.84 for R2, 0.62 for coefficients).
source: While we did observe some variation between forced and spontaneous walk in the R2 for regression of activity traces with walk, confidence intervals were overlapping for all brain regions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E) and cosine similarity was high (TH-DDC: 0.985 for R2, 0.978 for coefficients, Tdc: 0.96 for R2, 0.93 for coefficients, Trh: 0.84 for R2, 0.62 for coefficients) further suggesting that walking, whether spontaneous or forced, elicits a similar global state change of the brain.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supporting similarity between spontaneous and forced walk.

claim: Forced turns elicited different activity signatures from spontaneous turns.
source: By contrast, forced turns elicited different activity signatures from spontaneous turns (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing spontaneous and forced turning.

claim: Some components switched sign between spontaneous and forced turns (i.e., IPS-Y).
source: We found that some components switched sign (i.e., IPS-Y) while other components that showed little lateralization during spontaneous turns showed differences for forced turns (i.e., PPM2-VI, GNGm, FBcol) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a specific finding about differences in turning-related activity.

claim: The PPM2-LW component that showed lateralized activity during spontaneous walk was not lateralized during forced walk.
source: The PPM2-LW component that showed lateralized activity during spontaneous walk was not lateralized during forced walk.
evidence: This is a specific finding about a component's activity during different types of turns.

claim: Most components detected in both spontaneous and forced walk experiments appeared very similar.
source: Most components detected in both types of experiments appeared very similar as expected based on the analysis above (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing walk onset dynamics between conditions.

claim: Components with activity prior to spontaneous walk were either activated after walk had been triggered and/or their activity before walk was significantly different between spontaneous and forced walk.
source: Importantly, components with activity prior to spontaneous walk were either activated after walk had been triggered and/or their activity before walk was significantly different between spontaneous and forced walk (e.g., in areas around the esophagus, and in dorsal areas such as the γ3 compartment of the MB and the superior medial neuropil; Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding about differences in pre-walk activity between spontaneous and forced conditions.

claim: Locomotion and movement influence neural activity in many brain areas and many organisms.
source: Work over recent years has revealed that locomotion and movement influence neural activity in many brain areas and many organisms (Busse et al., 2017; Kaplan and Zimmer, 2020).
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous studies.

claim: Motor activity modulates not only local activity in specific brain regions, but also the global state of the brain.
source: Importantly, motor activity modulates not only local activity in specific brain regions, but also the global state of the brain.
evidence: This is a general statement about motor activity's effects on the brain.

claim: Movement elicits a global change in brain activity during spontaneous as well as forced walk in Drosophila.
source: Using fast in vivo whole brain calcium imaging in head-tethered behaving flies, we show that movement elicits a global change in brain activity during spontaneous as well as forced walk.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Walk activates several classes of neurons including excitatory, inhibitory, and aminergic, modulatory neurons.
source: Walk activates several classes of neurons including excitatory, inhibitory, and aminergic, modulatory neurons.
evidence: This is a summary finding about which neuron types are activated during walk.

claim: Except for serotonergic neurons which are inhibited during walk in some brain areas, neuronal activation was observed across all brain regions at the start of and during walking, but not during grooming or resting.
source: Except for serotonergic neurons which are inhibited during walk in some brain areas, we observed neuronal activation across all brain regions at the start of and during walking, but not during grooming or resting.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial and behavioral specificity of neural activation.

claim: Maps of dopaminergic activity during turning matched the spatial distribution of specific dopaminergic neurons.
source: For instance, we found that maps of dopaminergic activity during turning matched the spatial distribution of specific dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is a finding about matching functional and anatomical maps.

claim: Locomotion activates the brain by sending movement and proprioceptive information to specific regions (e.g., GNG) from where it activates all brain regions and neuron classes.
source: Based on the timing of activation and similarity between spontaneous and forced walk-induced brain activity, we propose that locomotion activates the brain by sending movement and proprioceptive information to specific regions (e.g., GNG) from where it activates all brain regions and neuron classes.
evidence: This is the main proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Light field microscopy allows for very fast imaging frame rates (up to 200 Hz for the whole brain).
source: While LFM allows for very fast imaging frame rates (up to 200 Hz for the whole brain), signal-to-noise ratio decreases with imaging speed.
evidence: This describes a technical capability of the imaging method.

claim: Signal-to-noise ratio decreases with imaging speed in light field microscopy.
source: While LFM allows for very fast imaging frame rates (up to 200 Hz for the whole brain), signal-to-noise ratio decreases with imaging speed.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the imaging method.

claim: The spatial resolution of light field imaging is inferior to that of confocal or volumetric multiphoton imaging.
source: Second, the spatial resolution of light field imaging is inferior to that of confocal or volumetric multiphoton imaging.
evidence: This is a comparison of imaging methods.

claim: Capturing the whole volume simultaneously with light field microscopy makes it easier to unmix signals using PCA/ICA approach, which partially compensates for the lower spatial resolution.
source: On the other hand, capturing the whole volume simultaneously makes it easier to unmix signals as we showed with our PCA/ICA approach, which partially compensates for the lower spatial resolution.
evidence: This explains an advantage of the light field method that compensates for a limitation.

claim: Averaging the activity in neuropile regions could hide information and reflect different activity patterns across single neurons.
source: Importantly, however, averaging the activity in neuropile regions could hide information, and reflect different activity patterns across single neurons.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the neuropil imaging approach.

claim: The data complement previous and future functional studies as imaging or manipulation of individual neurons provides only limited insights into the role and effect of a neuron in the complex and brain-wide dynamic neural network in which they are embedded.
source: We believe that our data complements previous and future functional studies as imaging or manipulation of individual neurons provides only limited insights into the role and effect of a neuron in the complex and brain-wide dynamic neural network in which they are embedded.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of whole brain imaging relative to single neuron studies.

claim: A combination of single neuron manipulation and whole brain imaging will likely lead to unexpected insights into the relationship between a neuron, global brain state, and a specific behavior.
source: In the future, a combination of single neuron manipulation and whole brain imaging will likely lead to unexpected insights into the relationship between a neuron, global brain state, and a specific behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Together with the now available whole brain EM connectome, the data provide a timely resource for the community of fly neuroscientists interested in linking neuronal activity to behavior.
source: Finally, together with the now available whole brain EM connectome, our data provide a timely resource for the community of fly neuroscientists interested in linking neuronal activity to behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the data as a resource.

claim: PCA/ICA as an unsupervised approach gave insights into the organization of whole brain activity underlying brain states.
source: Using PCA/ICA as an unsupervised approach gave us insights into the organization of whole brain activity underlying brain states.
evidence: This describes the value of the analysis method used.

claim: The PCA/ICA technique groups voxels that are correlated and thus misses more complex relationships.
source: This technique groups voxels that are correlated and thus misses more complex relationships.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the PCA/ICA method.

claim: The PCA/ICA method would not detect signals strongly corrupted by noise or different signals with the same spatial patterns.
source: Furthermore, our method would not detect signals strongly corrupted by noise or different signals with the same spatial patterns.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the PCA/ICA method.

claim: Some component-to-neuron correspondences are very speculative, while some components matched precisely the shape of known neurons or reproduced the shape of the only neuron types present in the same region for specific Gal4 lines.
source: Although some of these correspondences are very speculative, some components matched precisely the shape of known neurons (e.g., Figure 5), or reproduced the shape of the only neuron types present in the same region for specific Gal4 lines (e.g., MB compartments for dopamine Aso et al., 2014).
evidence: This discusses the confidence level in matching functional components to anatomical neurons.

claim: Several neurons matched to components were previously implicated in walking or its modulation.
source: Several of these neurons were previously implicated in walking or its modulation.
evidence: This relates the identified components to previous functional studies.

claim: EB–DA neurons show among the strongest and most reliable activity during walk and were shown to be involved in ethanol-induced locomotion, sleep regulation, and walk.
source: For instance, EB–DA, found in data from dopaminergic neurons, shows among the strongest and most reliable activity during walk. These neurons were shown to be involved in ethanol-induced locomotion (Kong et al., 2010), are involved in sleep regulation (Liang et al., 2016), and were shown more recently to be involved in walk (Fisher et al., 2022), with a timing relative to walk onset consistent with Figure 6.
evidence: This relates a functional component to previous studies on its function.

claim: Dopaminergic components in the MB recapitulate previous studies.
source: Dopaminergic components in the MB also recapitulate previous studies (Cohn et al., 2015; Siju et al., 2020).
evidence: This relates findings to previous studies on MB dopamine.

claim: The component PB–EB is consistent with neurons in the previously described head direction cells circuit shown to receive movement-related information during navigation.
source: The component PB–EB is consistent with neurons in the previously described head direction cells circuit shown to receive movement-related information during navigation (Lu et al., 2022; Lyu et al., 2022; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015).
evidence: This relates a component to previous studies on navigation circuits.

claim: The AVLPshell might be generated by a serotonergic neuron type of unknown function.
source: Among patterns not yet reported, the AVLPshell might be generated by a serotonergic neuron type of unknown function (e.g., Trh-F-100082; Chiang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about the identity of neurons underlying a component.

claim: Most components were correlated with walk, while others had an R2 indistinguishable from zero thus likely representing ongoing activity unrelated to walk or not captured by a linear model with a binary regressor for walk.
source: Although most components were correlated with walk, others had an R2 indistinguishable from zero thus likely representing ongoing activity unrelated to walk (Schaffer et al., 2021) or not captured by a linear model with a binary regressor for walk.
evidence: This interprets components that did not correlate with walk.

claim: The data provide an entry point to relate anatomical connectivity to brain states and activity in brain-wide neural networks.
source: Our data provide an entry point to relate anatomical connectivity to brain states and activity in brain-wide neural networks (Aimon and Grunwald Kadow, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the data for future studies.

claim: Whole brain connectomics in several small organisms including Drosophila has shown that neural networks extend across the entire brain with many pathways not predicted by single neuron or small motif imaging or manipulation of individual neurons.
source: Whole brain connectomics in several small organisms including Drosophila has shown that neural networks extend across the entire brain with many pathways not predicted by single neuron or small motif imaging or manipulation of individual neurons (Li et al., 2020; Scheffer et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This summarizes findings from connectomics studies.

claim: Whole brain imaging is a powerful method for observing brain-wide networks to study their contribution to behavior and ultimately to local activities within specific neurons or brain regions.
source: Whole brain imaging, as previously demonstrated in other model animals such as larval zebrafish, is a powerful method for observing these brain-wide networks to study their contribution to behavior and ultimately to local activities within specific neurons or brain regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of whole brain imaging methods.

claim: The fly (along with C. elegans and in the near future zebrafish) currently provides the important advantage of being able to combine activity maps with highly detailed anatomical maps from light microscopy with cellular resolution and whole brain EM connectomics with synaptic resolution.
source: While such data can be generated for other animals including humans, the fly (along with C. elegans and in the near future zebrafish) currently provides the important advantage of being able to combine such activity maps with highly detailed anatomical maps from light microscopy with cellular resolution and whole brain EM connectomics with synaptic resolution.
evidence: This explains the advantages of using Drosophila as a model system.

claim: DNs receive input from regions of the brain that are innervated by outputs from higher brain regions such as the MB and CC.
source: For instance, DNs receive input from regions of the brain that are innervated by outputs from higher brain regions such as the MB and CC (Hsu and Bhandawat, 2016).
evidence: This cites previous work on descending neuron connectivity.

claim: DN and AN innervation of the GNG is consistent with an important role of the GNG in motor control and motor feedback integration.
source: DN and AN innervation of the GNG is consistent with an important role of the GNG in motor control and motor feedback integration (Chen et al., 2023; Tsubouchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This interprets anatomical connectivity in terms of function and cites relevant studies.

claim: Neuromodulatory systems participate and show signatures of ongoing behavior in the adult fly brain.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, neuromodulatory systems participate and show signatures of ongoing behavior in the adult fly brain (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary statement about neuromodulatory neuron activity.

claim: Dopaminergic and octopaminergic neurons are broadly activated when the fly walks compared to rest or groom.
source: Dopaminergic and octopaminergic neurons are broadly activated when the fly walks compared to rest or groom (see Figure 3; Aimon et al., 2019; Siju et al., 2020), while serotonergic neurons show more complex activation patterns and timing with areas such as the AVLP being inhibited during walk (see Figure 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This summarizes findings about neuromodulatory neuron activity and cites previous studies.

claim: Serotonergic neurons show more complex activation patterns and timing with areas such as the AVLP being inhibited during walk.
source: Dopaminergic and octopaminergic neurons are broadly activated when the fly walks compared to rest or groom (see Figure 3; Aimon et al., 2019; Siju et al., 2020), while serotonergic neurons show more complex activation patterns and timing with areas such as the AVLP being inhibited during walk (see Figure 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This summarizes findings about serotonergic neuron activity.

claim: The data are consistent with data from other species and suggest that relationships between the activity of neuromodulatory neurons and locomotion are broadly conserved across species.
source: Our data are consistent with data from other species and suggest that relationships between the activity of neuromodulatory neurons and locomotion are broadly conserved across species.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing findings across species.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons are activated during locomotion in mammals, with some neurons reporting ongoing behavior while others show activity increase preceding behavior onset.
source: Dopaminergic neurons are activated during locomotion in mammals, with some neurons reporting ongoing behavior (Howe and Dombeck, 2016) while others show activity increase preceding behavior onset (Coddington and Dudman, 2019).
evidence: This cites previous studies on dopamine and locomotion in mammals.

claim: Although the majority of fly dopamine neurons are activated during ongoing behavior, some dopaminergic neurons are activated hundreds of milliseconds before the onset of walk in some trials.
source: We find that although the majority of fly dopamine neurons are activated during ongoing behavior, some dopaminergic neurons are activated hundreds of milliseconds before the onset of walk in some trials (e.g., WE-DA, M-Omega pattern, and γ1–3 compartments of the MB in some trials, Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of dopaminergic neuron activity.

claim: Norepinephrine/octopamine is a key neuromodulatory system involved in arousal in a variety of species.
source: Norepinephrine/octopamine is also a key neuromodulatory system involved in arousal in a variety of species (Berridge, 2008), with reports of an increase in activity of these neurons during locomotion in mammals (Gray et al., 2021; Kaufman et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This cites previous studies on norepinephrine/octopamine and arousal.

claim: In vertebrates, basal ganglia and brainstem aminergic neurons affect the cortico-basal ganglia–thalamic loops, and a disruption of these loops can result in a loss of motor control.
source: In vertebrates, basal ganglia and brainstem aminergic neurons affect the cortico-basal ganglia–thalamic loops. A disruption of these loops can result in a loss of motor control (Vicente et al., 2020).
evidence: This cites previous work on motor control circuits in vertebrates.

claim: Several octopaminergic neurons in the SEZ connect lower brain regions to the MB.
source: For example, several octopaminergic neurons in the SEZ connect lower brain regions to the MB (Busch et al., 2009).
evidence: This cites previous work on octopaminergic neuron connectivity.

claim: Serotonergic neurons show mixed roles in the control of motor behavior in different vertebrate species.
source: Interestingly, serotonergic neurons show mixed roles in the control of motor behavior in different vertebrate species (Dayan and Huys, 2015; Flaive et al., 2020; Vitrac and Benoit-Marand, 2017), as well as in insect, where it regulates various types of motor behaviors including feeding, aggression and larval locomotion (e.g., Aonuma, 2020; Helfrich-Förster, 2018; Ngai et al., 2019; Schoofs et al., 2018; Schoofs et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites previous studies on serotonin and motor behavior across species.

claim: Serotonin has been implicated in behavioral inhibition (e.g., patience) and as an opposing system to dopamine.
source: In particular, serotonin has been implicated in behavioral inhibition (e.g., patience; Doya et al., 2021) and as an opposing system to dopamine (Dayan, 2012).
evidence: This cites previous work on serotonin's role in behavior.

claim: The observation that serotonergic neurons in some brain regions such as the AVLP are inhibited during walk is consistent with serotonin's role in behavioral inhibition.
source: This is consistent with our observation that serotonergic neurons in some brain regions such as the AVLP are inhibited during walk (see also Howard et al., 2019 for serotonin in the VNC).
evidence: This interprets the finding about serotonergic neuron inhibition in the context of previous work.

claim: The AVLP receives input from ANs from the VNC conveying somatosensory information from the legs.
source: The AVLP receives input from ANs from the VNC conveying somatosensory information from the legs (Tsubouchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This cites previous work on AVLP connectivity.

claim: Calcium imaging revealed a spatial map for the AVLP and WED with neurons responding primarily to movement of fore-, mid-, or hindlegs.
source: Furthermore, calcium imaging revealed a spatial map for the AVLP and WED with neurons responding primarily to movement of fore-, mid-, or hindlegs (Chen et al., 2023; Tsubouchi et al., 2017), and the AVLP contains several descending neurons projecting toward the VNC (Namiki et al., 2022; Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites previous imaging and anatomical studies on the AVLP.

claim: The AVLP contains several descending neurons projecting toward the VNC.
source: Furthermore, calcium imaging revealed a spatial map for the AVLP and WED with neurons responding primarily to movement of fore-, mid-, or hindlegs (Chen et al., 2023; Tsubouchi et al., 2017), and the AVLP contains several descending neurons projecting toward the VNC (Namiki et al., 2022; Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites previous anatomical studies on the AVLP.

claim: Serotonin inhibition in the AVLP could be affecting a sensorimotor loop.
source: Serotonin inhibition in the AVLP could thus also be affecting a sensorimotor loop.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of serotonin inhibition.

claim: Key aspects of activity of neuromodulatory neurons during locomotion are conserved between mammals and insects despite their evolutionary distance.
source: Our study thus suggests that key aspects of activity of neuromodulatory neurons during locomotion are conserved between mammals and insects despite their evolutionary distance.
evidence: This is a conclusion about evolutionary conservation based on the findings.

claim: The results are most consistent with a model where proprioceptive, walking and leg sensory information are sent from the VNC into the GNG at the base of the fly's brain.
source: Our results are most consistent with a model where proprioceptive, walking and leg sensory information are sent from the VNC into the GNG at the base of the fly's brain.
evidence: This is the main proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Tuthill and colleagues recently identified some of the neural substrates in the VNC that receive, process and relay proprioceptive sensory information from the legs to the CNS.
source: Tuthill and colleagues recently identified some of the presumably many neural substrates in the VNC that receive, process and relay proprioceptive sensory information from the legs to the CNS (Agrawal et al., 2020; Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites recent work on proprioceptive circuits.

claim: The findings from Tuthill and colleagues provide strong support for an important role of proprioception in movement and locomotion control in the adult fly.
source: Their findings provide strong support for an important role of proprioception in movement and locomotion control in the adult fly.
evidence: This interprets previous findings about proprioception's role.

claim: Proprioceptive information is transmitted by ANs from the VNC to the central brain.
source: This information is transmitted by ANs from the VNC to the central brain.
evidence: This describes the pathway for proprioceptive information.

claim: A very recent study analyzed behavior-related activity of dozens of ANs labeled with specific Gal4 lines and concluded that ANs innervating regions such as the AVLP and GNG are poised to convey behavioral state and self-motion to several brain regions.
source: In particular, a very recent study analyzed behavior-related activity of dozens of ANs labeled with specific Gal4 lines (Chen et al., 2023) and came to the complementary conclusion that ANs innervating regions such as the AVLP and GNG are poised to convey behavioral state and self-motion to several brain regions.
evidence: This cites a recent study on ascending neuron function.

claim: Grooming or forced walk on a treadmill does not require an active brain.
source: While grooming or forced walk on a treadmill does not require an active brain, lesions of the neck connectives as we have carried out dramatically decrease spontaneous walking in locusts (Kien, 1990a; Kien, 1990b), indicating that at least initiation of walk can be dependent on the brain.
evidence: This cites previous work on the brain's role in walk initiation.

claim: Lesions of the neck connectives dramatically decrease spontaneous walking in locusts, indicating that at least initiation of walk can be dependent on the brain.
source: While grooming or forced walk on a treadmill does not require an active brain, lesions of the neck connectives as we have carried out dramatically decrease spontaneous walking in locusts (Kien, 1990a; Kien, 1990b), indicating that at least initiation of walk can be dependent on the brain.
evidence: This cites previous work and interprets its implications.

claim: A cat with a severed spinal cord maintains a highly coordinated walk pattern when forced to walk on a treadmill.
source: On the other hand, a cat with a severed spinal cord, like our fly with a severed VNC, maintains a highly coordinated walk pattern when forced to walk on a treadmill (Afelt, 1974).
evidence: This cites previous work on spinal cord lesions in cats.

claim: Coordinated walk appears to mainly depend on central pattern generators in the spinal cord or VNC and is largely independent of brain input.
source: Thus, coordinated walk appears to mainly depend on central pattern generators in the spinal cord or VNC and is largely independent of brain input.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited studies and the current findings.

claim: The result that whole brain activity induced by spontaneous walking was similar to the activity observed by forcing the animal to walk on a rotating rod is consistent with the interpretation that walk itself and not top-down motor control is responsible for the majority of activity observed in actively moving animals' brains.
source: Surprisingly, whole brain activity induced by spontaneous walking was similar to the activity we observed by forcing the animal to walk on a rotating rod (Figure 7). This result and our finding that the activity induced by walk in the GNG stems in a large part from axons are consistent with the interpretation that walk itself and not top-down motor control is responsible for the majority of activity observed in actively moving animals' brains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spontaneous vs. forced walk comparison.

claim: Neurons connecting lower to higher areas (e.g., neurons underlying the PENP-CL, GNG-SLP, and WPNb components, as well as octopaminergic neurons) could relay walk information to higher areas once the walk signals reach the brain.
source: Once the walk signals reach the brain, neurons connecting lower to higher areas (e.g., neurons underlying the PENP-CL, GNG-SLP, and WPNb components, as well as octopaminergic neurons) could relay this information to higher areas.
evidence: This is a speculation about how walk information spreads through the brain.

claim: The data that inhibitory neurons are also broadly activated is inconsistent with the idea that broad brain activation arises due to a global disinhibition during periods of walking.
source: Interestingly, our data that inhibitory neurons are also broadly activated is inconsistent with the idea that broad brain activation arises due to a global disinhibition during periods of walking (Benjamin et al., 2010), although additional experiments will be necessary to ensure that activity in individual regions is not dominated by a small subset of activated neurons in a sea of inhibited neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inhibitory neuron findings and cites an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Several brain components and small subregions, for instance in the posterior slope, were activated hundreds of milliseconds before the fly started to walk.
source: Importantly, however, we identified several brain components and small subregions, for instance in the posterior slope, that were activated hundreds of milliseconds before the fly started to walk (see Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding about pre-walk activity in specific brain regions.

claim: Activity before walk onset in some areas was delayed in forced walk and started only when the fly had started to move, suggesting a potential role of these areas in initiating walk.
source: This activity was delayed in forced walk and started only when the fly had started to move. This suggests a potential role of these areas in initiating walk.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing differences between spontaneous and forced walk.

claim: Activity before walk onset could also be due to preparatory movements that were not detected as walk, or represent the activity of neurons downstream of neurons responsible for triggering walk.
source: Activity before walk onset could also be due to preparatory movements that were not detected as walk (Ache et al., 2019), or represent the activity of neurons downstream of neurons responsible for triggering walk.
evidence: This presents alternative interpretations of pre-walk activity.

claim: One important concept to explain the role of behavioral state-dependent neural modulation is 'active sensation'.
source: One important concept to explain the role of behavioral state-dependent neural modulation is 'active sensation' (Busse et al., 2017).
evidence: This introduces a concept from previous work.

claim: Ongoing movement can shape how neurons respond to visual, somatosensory, and possibly other sensory stimuli.
source: Essentially, ongoing movement can shape how neurons respond to visual, somatosensory, and possibly other sensory stimuli (Chapman et al., 2018; Cruz et al., 2021; Fenk et al., 2021; Henschke et al., 2021; Wolpert et al., 2011).
evidence: This cites previous work on active sensation.

claim: Extracellular recordings from mouse V1 neurons walking on a ball showed that evoked visual responses differ in neurons of moving animals and those of still animals.
source: For example, extracellular recordings from mouse V1 neurons walking on a ball showed that evoked visual responses differ in neurons of moving animals and those of still animals (Dadarlat and Stryker, 2017).
evidence: This cites a previous study on movement and visual responses in mice.

claim: Fly visual neurons respond more strongly to stimuli during walk or flight.
source: Similarly, fly visual neurons respond more strongly to stimuli during walk or flight (Chiappe et al., 2010; Maimon et al., 2010; Suver et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites previous studies on movement and visual responses in flies.

claim: The increase in whole brain activity is elicited at walk onset and maintained afterwards.
source: Our data indicate that the increase whole brain activity is elicited at walk onset and maintained afterwards (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding about the temporal dynamics of brain activity during walk.

claim: The overall increase in brain activity is not larger during forced walk as compared to spontaneous walk.
source: Since the overall increase in brain activity is not larger during forced walk as compared to spontaneous walk, our data also suggest that global brain activity does not generally represent a mismatch, or error signal, between actual and predicted proprioceptive feedback during walk.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between spontaneous and forced walk.

claim: Global brain activity does not generally represent a mismatch, or error signal, between actual and predicted proprioceptive feedback during walk.
source: Since the overall increase in brain activity is not larger during forced walk as compared to spontaneous walk, our data also suggest that global brain activity does not generally represent a mismatch, or error signal, between actual and predicted proprioceptive feedback during walk.
evidence: This is an interpretation ruling out a prediction error hypothesis.

claim: Movement specific information reaches the brain and modulates brain activity widely.
source: These observations support the conclusion that movement specific information reach the brain and modulate brain activity widely.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Movement-related information could serve multiple purposes from uncoupling of sensory-to-motor information (own movement vs. movement of environment) to learning of complex movements.
source: Such information could serve multiple purposes from uncoupling of sensory-to-motor information, that is own movement vs. movement of environment, to learning of complex movements (Lu et al., 2022).
evidence: This speculates about the functional roles of movement-related brain activity.

claim: Drosophila brain activity is globally correlated with locomotion representing a global change in brain state.
source: As for other animals, Drosophila brain activity is globally correlated with locomotion representing a global change in brain state.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The results challenge the assumption that most of the activity is related to decision-making, top-down motor control, or prediction error detection from sensory feedback and instead suggest that walk itself and somatosensory bottom-up stimuli are largely responsible.
source: However, our results challenge the assumption that most of the activity is related to decision-making, top-down motor control, or prediction error detection from sensory feedback and instead suggest that walk itself and somatosensory bottom-up stimuli are largely responsible.
evidence: This is a main conclusion that challenges previous assumptions.

claim: The data provide a novel resource for generating new hypotheses regarding the brain-behavior loop and for dissecting the neural circuits and computations underpinning it.
source: Altogether, our data provide a novel resource for generating new hypotheses regarding the brain-behavior loop and for dissecting the neural circuits and computations underpinning it.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the data for future research.
